data:
Token Broker gives coding agents such as Claude Code their own GitHub identity. A developer or a GitHub Actions workflow proves who they are, and the broker hands back a one-hour token of the agent GitHub App for a single repository. The app’s private key never leaves the broker.
Getting startedInstall the client and get your first agent token, or deploy the broker. GuidesSet up the GitHub Apps, use tokens in Actions, sign commits, set review rules. ReferenceClient commands and variables, broker configuration, endpoints, Helm values, metrics. ConceptsThe two auth paths and the security model. The README, the longer docs and the architecture decision records stay in the repository: docs/ and the ADRs.

How the broker decides who gets a token, and what an agent can and cannot reach.
ArchitectureThe two auth paths and how a token is issued. Security modelWhat the agent never sees, and where the plugin stops. The decisions behind this design are recorded as ADRs in the repository.

Coding agents need to push code and open pull requests. Giving them a developer’s credentials makes every agent action look like the developer’s, and a prompt injection then holds everything the developer can do. Token Broker gives the agent its own GitHub identity instead: a GitHub App. Its commits and pull requests show up as [bot] and need a human review.
data.one-key-one-place#One key, one place: An app can mint installation tokens only with its private key. The key lives in the broker alone. Agents, containers and workstations ask the broker for a token and never see the key.
data.parts#Parts: Broker: a small stateless Go service, run as a Helm chart with two replicas. It has no database and never calls the Kubernetes API. Client scripts: agent-token and the helpers built on it. See Client commands. Claude Code plugin, Dev Container Feature and agent-run: three ways to put the client into the agent’s environment. See Getting started. Setup details: Set up the GitHub Apps. Endpoints and errors: Endpoints.
data.two-auth-paths#Two auth paths: Caller Proves identity with Endpoint Developer (local agent) user token of a permission-less login app, via device flow POST /token GitHub Actions workflow the workflow’s OIDC token POST /token/actions (or /token) Developer. agent-token --login runs GitHub’s device flow with the login app, an app with no permissions at all. It only proves who the developer is. The login token lives 8 hours in the developer’s cache. The broker asks GitHub whether that user has write access to the requested repository and refuses otherwise: a developer can hand the agent only repositories they could push to themselves. Workflow. The workflow requests an OIDC token with the audience the broker expects and sends it to the broker. The broker verifies it against GitHub’s issuer. A workflow gets a token only for the repository it runs in, optionally limited to certain refs and workflows. /token/actions accepts nothing but these tokens, so a public route can forward it while everything else stays internal.
data.what-the-token-is#What the token is:
In both cases the broker then:
checks that the repository belongs to one of the configured organizations; signs an app JWT with the private key and looks up the app’s installation on the repository, refusing if the app is not installed there; mints an installation token for that one repository, with the configured permissions (default: contents, pull requests and issues write, metadata read). The token lives one hour. Clients fetch tokens on demand, per repository, at the moment git, gh or the GitHub MCP server need one, and cache them. Every issued or denied token is logged: who, which repository, why.

data.exposure-of-the-broker#Exposure of the b:
The device-flow client ID is public, so a reachable broker invites phishing. Keep /token internal. Only /token/actions is built for public exposure: it accepts Actions OIDC tokens and nothing else. GitHub never calls the broker; it needs outbound access to api.github.com and token.actions.githubusercontent.com only. Run it behind TLS.
Limits: commits made with local git are unsigned, so on branches that require signatures use agent-commit or squash-merge.
data.host-versus-container#Host versus contai: Host with the plugin Container or Dev Container Developer credentials (~/.ssh, gh login) reachable by the agent not mounted Enforcement command-text guard the container’s contents Network unrestricted Dev Container: egress firewall with an allowlist On the host, deny the agent read access to ~/.ssh, ~/.config/gh and ~/.cache/agent-token. For isolation run the agent with agent-run or in the Dev Container. The Dev Container’s firewall cannot be lifted by the agent, but your forwarded SSH agent can still sign; use agent-run for full isolation. Skipping Claude’s permission prompts is reasonable only with the firewall active.
data.humans-stay-in-the-loop#Humans stay in t: The agent app can approve pull requests, and with contents write its approvals would count toward required reviews. Every repository it is installed on must therefore require a code owner review and have a CODEOWNERS file that names human teams: bots cannot be code owners. See Set review rules.
data.the-plugin-is-a-guardrail-not-a-sandbox#:
The Claude Code plugin tells Claude to use agent tokens and blocks git commit, git push and a bare gh by matching command text. A command like env git push, /usr/bin/git push or a script that pushes gets through and uses the developer’s credentials. The block also follows the session, not the directory: after a cd into another repository it still applies, and a session started outside an agent-token repository stays unguarded.
Repository admins can edit topics by hand. A wrong topic costs a failed call and nothing more, because the broker refuses tokens where the app is not installed.
data.what-the-agent-never-sees#What the agent: The agent app’s private key and the login app’s client secret. They exist only in the broker. The developer’s own credentials. Agent commits and API calls use agent tokens, so they cannot act as the developer. An agent token is limited to one repository, lives one hour and carries only the configured permissions. Metadata aside, the default is contents, pull requests and issues. It has no workflow, administration, secrets or status permissions, so it cannot edit CI, manage the repository or report a required check as green.

data:
Pick how your agent runs. All paths need the broker URL from your deployment. If your organization publishes it as the Actions variable AGENT_TOKEN_BROKER_URL, the Claude Code plugin finds it itself.
Claude Code pluginThe main path: Claude Code on your host, acting as the agent app. HomebrewInstall the client scripts with brew. Install scriptInstall a pinned release without a package manager. ContainerRun Claude Code in a container with only the agent token. Dev ContainerAdd the agent-token Dev Container Feature. KubernetesDeploy the broker with the Helm chart.
Install the agent-token plugin so Claude Code on your host commits and calls GitHub as the agent app instead of as you.
data.before-you-start#Before you start: jq, gh (logged in), curl and git on the host. The agent app is installed on your repository, and the repository carries the topic agent-token-broker. The broker’s URL. The plugin looks for it in this order: the TOKEN_BROKER_URL environment variable, the plugin option broker_url, the Actions variable AGENT_TOKEN_BROKER_URL of the repository’s organization, read with your gh. Repository variables are ignored, so a repository admin cannot send your login to another server. Only https:// URLs are accepted.
data.install#Install:
claude plugin marketplace add pflege-de-labs/token-broker claude plugin install agent-token@pflege-de-token-broker To set the broker URL at install time, add --config broker_url=https://. You can also set it later in Claude Code with /config.
The plugin carries the client scripts: its bin/ directory is on the PATH of Claude’s Bash tool. Your own PATH comes first, so a Homebrew or script install wins. The plugin tracks main, while Homebrew, the install script and the containers install pinned releases. Marketplace auto-update is off by default; update with claude plugin update agent-token@pflege-de-token-broker.
data.log-in#Log in:
Once per 8 hours, in the Claude Code prompt:
! agent-token --login The first login prints a code for https://github.com/login/device. The login token is cached in ~/.cache/agent-token/login.json.
data.what-happens-in-a-session#What happens i:
A SessionStart hook checks whether the repository carries the topic agent-token-broker. If it does, Claude is told to commit and call GitHub with agent tokens, and the hook adds the result of agent-token --check. In every other directory the plugin stays silent.
In such a session a PreToolUse hook blocks Bash commands that contain git commit or git push, and a bare gh where agent-gh exists. Claude uses agent-commit and agent-gh instead.
The plugin is a guardrail, not a sandbox. The hook matches command text, so env git push or a script that pushes get through with your credentials. For isolation use the container or the Dev Container. See the security model.

data: agent-run starts Claude Code in a container whose only GitHub credential is an agent token for one repository. Your SSH keys, gh login, git config and the broker login token stay on the host.
data.before-you-start#Before you start: podman, curl, jq and git on the host. agent-token on your PATH (Homebrew or install script). A clone of the token-broker repository, which holds agent-run and the image definition in container/.
data.configure#Configure: export TOKEN_BROKER_URL=https:// export AGENT_APP_SLUG= export CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=
data.limits#Limits: The token covers one repository: fetching private dependencies from other repositories, such as Go modules, fails. Commits are unsigned; merge agent pull requests with squash. After 8 hours the login token expires and the next renewal prints a device code on the terminal.
data.run#Run:
From inside a checkout (a clone or a git worktree):
/path/to/token-broker/agent-run # repository from the `origin` remote /path/to/token-broker/agent-run my-org/my-repo # explicit repository /path/to/token-broker/agent-run -p "fix the failing test" # arguments go to claude agent-run:
gets an agent token with agent-token (device flow on first use) and renews it every 45 minutes while the session runs; the container reads it from a read-only file; mounts the checkout at the same path, plus the main repository’s .git for worktrees; rewrites GitHub SSH remotes to HTTPS, so git pushes with the agent token; sets the commit identity to [bot] <+[bot]@users.noreply.github.com>; keeps Claude Code’s settings in the named volume agent-claude; maps your user to the container user, so files keep your ownership; installs the repository’s toolchain from mise.toml or .tool-versions before Claude starts. AGENT_IMAGE selects another image. AGENT_PODMAN_ARGS adds podman flags, for example --entrypoint sh for a shell instead of Claude.
data.toolchains#Toolchains:
The image holds only what every repository needs: git, gh, jq, curl, make, unzip, ripgrep, shellcheck, python3 and mise. Everything else comes from the repository’s mise config at its pinned versions. Installs and caches live in the volumes agent-mise and agent-cache, so only the first session per version downloads. A repository without a mise config gets no extra tools.
agent-run trusts the mise config of the mounted checkout only. A failed mise install prints a warning and Claude starts anyway.
Never mount cloud credentials (~/.aws, kubeconfigs): they are developer credentials. Let the agent write code and run terraform plan in CI instead.

data:
The agent-token Dev Container Feature installs the client scripts, pinned to a release, into a devcontainer. It is published in pflege-de-labs/devcontainer-features.
The token-broker repository’s own .devcontainer/ is a working setup to copy. It:
installs the scripts with the Feature (pinned by digest in devcontainer.json); sets the bot identity and installs Claude Code and the toolchain from mise.toml; adds a SessionStart hook as managed settings, which reminds you when the login is missing; limits outbound traffic with an egress firewall to an allowlist of domains plus the broker host. On first attach the terminal shows a device code; log in there. With Podman, set "dev.containers.dockerPath": "podman" in your VS Code settings.
data.things-to-know#Things to know: Everything committed or pushed in the container goes out as the agent app’s bot, including commits from the VS Code Source Control view. Commit as yourself from the host. The agent commits with agent-commit, so branches that require signatures accept them. VS Code forwards your credentials into devcontainers. The setup turns off git.terminalAuthentication and github.gitAuthentication, overrides GIT_AUTHOR_* and GIT_COMMITTER_*, and has the credential helper answer quit=1 when it has no token. Your SSH agent is still forwarded: the firewall blocks port 22, but it can still sign. For full isolation use agent-run. A git worktree does not work as the workspace, because its .git points outside the mount. Open a clone. Network access beyond the allowlist needs a change to allowed-domains and a rebuild. For an image without the Feature, see Use the scripts in your own image. To use the GitHub MCP server, see agent-github-mcp.

data:
Install the client scripts on macOS or Linux with Homebrew. The formula depends on jq and gh. Homebrew loads formulae from a third-party tap only after you trust it with brew trust.
brew tap pflege-de-labs/token-broker https://github.com/pflege-de-labs/token-broker brew trust --tap pflege-de-labs/token-broker brew install agent-token Set the broker URL and request a token:
export TOKEN_BROKER_URL=https://<broker> agent-token my-org/my-repo # prints a 1h agent token The first run prints a code for https://github.com/login/device. The login token is cached for 8 hours in ~/.cache/agent-token/login.json (mode 600), so later runs need no browser.
Homebrew installs a pinned release. To use the scripts from Claude Code without managing the install yourself, use the plugin.
Without a container, deny the agent read access to ~/.ssh, ~/.config/gh and ~/.cache/agent-token. See client commands for what each script does.

Install the client scripts from a release tarball, without a package manager.
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pflege-de-labs/token-broker/main/scripts/install.sh | bash The script:
downloads agent-token-.tar.gz from the release and verifies its sha256 against the release’s checksums.txt; installs the scripts into $PREFIX/bin, PREFIX defaulting to ~/.local; installs agent-gh as agent-gh, never as gh on the host; never changes your global git config. Make sure $PREFIX/bin is on your PATH.
data.choose-the-install-directory#Choose the: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pflege-de-labs/token-broker/main/scripts/install.sh \ | PREFIX=/opt/agent bash Every v* release carries agent-token-.tar.gz (the scripts in bin/) and checksums.txt. The script needs bash, curl and jq; gh is needed for agent-gh.

data:
Deploy the broker with the Helm chart. Create the two GitHub Apps first, as described in Set up the GitHub Apps.
The image is ghcr.io/pflege-de-labs/token-broker; the chart is published to oci://ghcr.io/pflege-de-labs/charts/token-broker. The chart has no deployment-specific defaults.
data.2-write-the-values#2. Write the values: existingSecret: token-broker-credentials config: appId: "" org: my-org loginClientId: "" config.org is a comma-separated list; only repositories of these organizations get tokens.
data.4-expose-it#4. Expose it:
Developers and runners with internal network access reach the broker through ingress or httpRoute. Keep that route internal: the device-flow client ID is public, so a reachable broker invites phishing. Workflows on GitHub-hosted runners need the public actionsRoute, which forwards only POST on one path to /token/actions (details).
The broker needs outbound access to api.github.com and token.actions.githubusercontent.com only; GitHub never calls it. Run it behind TLS.
Check it with GET /healthz and GET /readyz; /readyz succeeds when GitHub accepts the app key. See Helm values and broker configuration.

data:
Each guide covers one task.
Set up the GitHub Apps Get agent tokens in GitHub Actions Sign agent commits Set review rules Use the scripts in your own image

Workflows exchange their OIDC token for an agent token. Where the broker is reachable decides which runners can use it.
Runner Broker endpoint Chart GitHub-hosted public POST /token/actions actionsRoute self-hosted with internal network access internal POST /token/actions (or /token) httpRoute or the Service /token/actions accepts Actions OIDC tokens and nothing else, so actionsRoute can be public: it forwards exactly one path, POST only, and developer logins, probes and metrics stay internal.
data.restrict-refs-and-workflows#Restrict ref:
By default any workflow in a repository the app is installed on may get a token. Two chart values narrow that. Both are lists of patterns where * matches any characters, including /:
config: actionsOidc: # `ref` claim: only the default branch and release tags allowedRefs: [refs/heads/main, "refs/tags/v*"] # `job_workflow_ref` claim: only a shared agent workflow allowedWorkflows: ["my-org/agent-workflows/.github/workflows/agent.yml@*"] A request must match one pattern of each configured list. Empty lists apply no restriction. Pull request runs carry ref: refs/pull//merge, so allowedRefs without refs/pull/* blocks agents on pull requests.
data.workflow#Workflow:
Workflows pick runner and broker URL from Actions variables, so one workflow serves both setups:
jobs: agent: runs-on: ${{ vars.AGENT_RUNNER || 'ubuntu-latest' }} permissions: id-token: write contents: read steps: - id: agent env: BROKER: ${{ vars.AGENT_TOKEN_BROKER_ACTIONS_URL }} run: | oidc=$(curl -fsS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_TOKEN" \ "$ACTIONS_ID_TOKEN_REQUEST_URL&audience=token-broker" | jq -r .value) token=$(curl -fsS "$BROKER/token/actions" -H "Authorization: Bearer $oidc" \ -d "{\"repo\":\"$GITHUB_REPOSITORY\"}" | jq -r .token) echo "::add-mask::$token" echo "token=$token" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT" - uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 with: github_token: ${{ steps.agent.outputs.token }} The audience must match ACTIONS_OIDC_AUDIENCE (default token-broker). AGENT_TOKEN_BROKER_ACTIONS_URL is the organization’s Actions variable with the broker’s base URL for workflows: the public route for GitHub-hosted runners, or the internal URL for self-hosted runners. The workflow appends /token/actions. AGENT_TOKEN_BROKER_URL is the internal URL for developer machines (Dev Container); the public route does not serve their logins.
The token covers only the repository the workflow runs in: the broker requires both the repository claim and sub to name the requested repository. sub is either the classic repo:owner/name:… or the immutable repo:owner@ID/name@ID:…, whose IDs are checked against the signed ID claims. The token expires after one hour.

data:
The broker needs two organization-owned GitHub Apps. Settings live under Organization settings → Developer settings → GitHub Apps.
Agent app Login app Purpose Identity agents commit, push and open pull requests as Proves who a developer is (device flow) Repository permissions Contents RW, Pull requests RW, Issues RW, Metadata R none Organization / account permissions none none Device flow off on Installed on selected repositories not needed Broker config GITHUB_APP_ID, private key LOGIN_APP_CLIENT_ID, client secret
data.agent-app#Agent app:
The owner is the organization, not a personal account. Where can this app be installed: only on this account. Webhook: active unchecked. The broker receives no events. Identifying and authorizing users: no callback URL, Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation off, Enable Device Flow off. User tokens of this app would act as the developer. Repository permissions: Contents, Pull requests and Issues Read and write, Metadata Read-only. Everything else No access, in particular: Workflows, so an agent cannot edit CI to escalate. Administration, Secrets, Environments and Actions, so it cannot manage repositories or secrets. Checks and Statuses, so it cannot report a required check as green. Organization and Account permissions: all No access. Subscribe to events: none. Private keys: generate one key. It goes only into the broker Secret as private-key.pem, never into a repository secret or onto a laptop. Delete the downloaded file afterwards. Install App on Only select repositories: the repositories agents may work on. The app is not a bypass actor in any ruleset. Note the App ID (config.appId). Every repository the app is installed on must also set review rules.
The broker requests only the four permissions per token, so granting more to the app widens nothing for agents. AGENT_PERMISSIONS (chart: config.agentPermissions) changes that set; every installation must have accepted each permission in it, or GitHub refuses the token. Keep the app minimal: the private key alone can mint tokens with everything the app has.
data.broker-secret-and-values#Broker Secret a: kubectl create secret generic token-broker-credentials \ --from-file=private-key.pem=.private-key.pem \ --from-literal=login-client-secret="$LOGIN_CLIENT_SECRET" existingSecret: token-broker-credentials config: appId: "" org: my-org loginClientId: "" Prefer an external secret manager over creating the Secret by hand.
data.commit-identity-of-the-agent#Commit iden:
The bot’s commit email uses the bot user ID, not the App ID:
id=$(gh api "/users/%5Bbot%5D" --jq .id) echo "[bot] <${id}+[bot]@users.noreply.github.com>" Commits created through the API with an installation token are signed by GitHub and attributed to this identity automatically.
data.login-app#Login app: The owner is the organization; install only on this account. Webhook: active unchecked. Repository, Organization and Account permissions: all No access. Enable Device Flow on. Expire user authorization tokens on: login tokens live 8 hours. Callback URL: none needed for device flow. If the form insists, use the broker URL. Request user authorization (OAuth) during installation off; the app need not be installed. Note the Client ID (config.loginClientId). The broker serves it to clients at /login-app. Generate one client secret. It goes only into the broker Secret as login-client-secret.
data.rotate-credentials#Rotate credentials: Agent app private key: generate a new key, update the Secret, roll the broker (the chart’s checksum annotation only covers a chart-managed Secret), then delete the old key. Login app client secret: same order. Developer login tokens stay valid; they are checked against the app, not the secret.

data: If you cannot use the Dev Container Feature, install the client scripts in your image yourself.
data.build-run-log-in#Build, run, log in: podman build -t agent-dev . podman volume create agent-token-cache podman run -it --name agent-dev \ -v agent-token-cache:/root/.cache/agent-token \ -v "$PWD":/work -w /work agent-dev bash # inside, once per 8h: agent-token --login From another terminal: podman exec -it agent-dev agent-token --login.
data.install-a-pinned-release#Install a pinne:
Check the tarball against its sha256 from the release’s checksums.txt:
FROM docker.io/library/debian:bookworm-slim RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends bash ca-certificates curl git gh jq \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* ARG AGENT_TOKEN_VERSION= ARG AGENT_TOKEN_SHA256= RUN curl -fsSL -o /tmp/agent-token.tgz \ "https://github.com/pflege-de-labs/token-broker/releases/download/v$AGENT_TOKEN_VERSION/agent-token-$AGENT_TOKEN_VERSION.tar.gz" \ && echo "$AGENT_TOKEN_SHA256 /tmp/agent-token.tgz" | sha256sum -c - \ && tar -xzf /tmp/agent-token.tgz -C /tmp \ && install -m 755 /tmp/bin/agent-token /tmp/bin/agent-token-git-credential /tmp/bin/agent-github-mcp /tmp/bin/agent-commit /usr/local/bin/ \ && install -m 755 /tmp/bin/agent-gh /usr/local/bin/gh \ && rm -rf /tmp/agent-token.tgz /tmp/bin RUN git config --system credential.https://github.com.helper '' \ && git config --system --add credential.https://github.com.helper '!agent-token-git-credential' \ && git config --system credential.https://github.com.useHttpPath true \ && git config --system url.https://github.com/.insteadOf git@github.com: \ && git config --system --add url.https://github.com/.insteadOf ssh://git@github.com/ ENV TOKEN_BROKER_URL=https:// Debian’s gh lands in /usr/bin, after /usr/local/bin in PATH. Add Claude Code and your toolchain as usual.
data.what-the-image-needs#What the image need:
bash, curl, jq, git, gh; github-mcp-server only for the MCP server.
The scripts in /usr/local/bin, with agent-gh installed as gh. It must come before the real gh in PATH; the wrapper finds the real one itself.
TOKEN_BROKER_URL in the environment.
System git config:
# The empty value drops inherited helpers (store, osxkeychain, gh) for github.com. git config --system credential.https://github.com.helper '' git config --system --add credential.https://github.com.helper '!agent-token-git-credential' # Without the path git cannot say which repo it needs a token for. git config --system credential.https://github.com.useHttpPath true # Credential helpers only work over HTTPS. git config --system url.https://github.com/.insteadOf git@github.com: git config --system --add url.https://github.com/.insteadOf ssh://git@github.com/ A volume for ~/.cache/agent-token, so the login survives container restarts. It holds the developer’s login token (8 hours) and agent tokens (1 hour); keep it per developer, never shared.
The agent should act only as the agent app, so the wrapper refuses gh auth login, refresh and setup-git. Outside a checkout, gh auth status reports the agent-token login. Commands without one target repository (gh api orgs/...) get no agent token and fail unauthenticated, by design.

data:
The agent app has contents write permission, so its approvals would count toward required reviews. Bots cannot be code owners, so a code owner review closes the gap. Every repository the app is installed on therefore needs:
A CODEOWNERS file that names human teams. A rule on the default branch that requires a code owner review. No bypass for the agent app in any ruleset. Agent commits and pull requests then show up as the app’s bot and need a human review.
If you require signed commits, merge agent pull requests with squash, so the commit on the protected branch is created and signed by GitHub. See Sign agent commits.
See also Set up the GitHub Apps.

git commit in a container makes unsigned commits: GitHub signs app commits only when it creates them itself. Rulesets with required_signatures then block them on protected branches. Squash merges still work, because GitHub signs the squash commit.
agent-commit sends the staged changes to the GraphQL mutation createCommitOnBranch and moves the local branch onto the signed commit:
git add -A agent-commit -m "feat: something" -m "Body." # or -F <file> It pushes as it commits; there is no separate git push. A branch missing on origin is created at HEAD, which must already be on GitHub. It refuses if the local branch has commits that origin lacks, and for new executables or mode changes: the API has no file mode, so new files land as 100644. Commit those with git commit and merge with squash. It creates no merge commits; rebase onto the base branch instead. AGENT_COMMIT_MODE=local turns it into plain git commit, for repositories that do not want API commits. In the Dev Container, /etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md tells Claude Code to use agent-commit. With the Claude Code plugin, the guard blocks git commit and points Claude here.
See agent-commit for the full reference.

Complete lists for lookup.
Client commandsagent-token, agent-gh, agent-commit and the other scripts. Client environmentVariables the client scripts read. Broker configurationEnvironment variables of the broker. EndpointsHTTP API of the broker. Helm valuesValues of the token-broker chart. MetricsPrometheus metrics the broker exports.

The broker reads its configuration from environment variables. The Helm chart renders them from its values.
Variable Chart value Default Meaning GITHUB_APP_ID config.appId App ID of the agent app. Required. GITHUB_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_FILE Secret key private-key.pem Path to the agent app’s private key. Required. GITHUB_ORG config.org Comma-separated organizations; only their repositories get tokens. Required. LOGIN_APP_CLIENT_ID config.loginClientId Client ID of the login app. Required. LOGIN_APP_CLIENT_SECRET Secret key login-client-secret Client secret of the login app. Required. ACTIONS_OIDC_AUDIENCE config.actionsOidc.audience token-broker Audience workflows must request. ACTIONS_OIDC_ISSUER config.actionsOidc.issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com Issuer of Actions OIDC tokens. ACTIONS_ALLOWED_REFS config.actionsOidc.allowedRefs empty: any Comma-separated glob patterns for the ref claim. ACTIONS_ALLOWED_WORKFLOWS config.actionsOidc.allowedWorkflows empty: any Comma-separated glob patterns for the job_workflow_ref claim. AGENT_PERMISSIONS config.agentPermissions contents:write,pull_requests:write,issues:write,metadata:read Permissions of every agent token, as name:level,..., level read or write. LISTEN_ADDR :8080 Listen address. GITHUB_API_URL config.apiUrl https://api.github.com GitHub API base URL. In glob patterns * matches any characters, including /. AGENT_PERMISSIONS replaces the default set: list all permissions, and the agent app must have been granted each of them, or GitHub refuses the token. An invalid entry stops the broker at start.
The broker needs outbound access to api.github.com and token.actions.githubusercontent.com only. It logs every issued and denied token as a structured log line with the caller and the repository.

The client scripts live in bin/ of every agent-token-.tar.gz release asset and of the Claude Code plugin. They need bash, curl and jq. All of them read the client environment.
Script Role agent-token Device-flow login, login check, token per repository with a cache agent-token-git-credential git credential helper for github.com agent-gh Wrapper for gh that sets GH_TOKEN for the target repository agent-github-mcp Starts the local github-mcp-server with a token for the current repository agent-commit Commits the staged changes through the GitHub API, so GitHub signs them
data.agent-commit#agent-commit: agent-commit -m [-m ]... agent-commit -F Commits the staged changes through GraphQL createCommitOnBranch, so GitHub signs the commit, pushes it and moves the local branch onto it. Details and limits: Sign agent commits. AGENT_COMMIT_MODE=local runs plain git commit with the arguments instead.
data.agent-gh#agent-gh:
Runs the real gh with GH_TOKEN set to an agent token for the target repository. The target is the --repo/-R flag, else GH_REPO, else the origin remote. Install it as gh in containers, ahead of the real gh in PATH; on the host the install script installs it as agent-gh.
gh auth login, refresh and setup-git are refused. Outside a checkout, gh auth status reports the agent-token login. Commands without one target repository (gh api orgs/...) get no agent token and run with gh’s own authentication, if any.
data.agent-github-mcp#agent-github-mcp:
Starts github-mcp-server stdio with an agent token for the origin repository of the current directory; further arguments go to the server. Register it with Claude Code:
claude mcp add --scope user github -- agent-github-mcp --toolsets repos,issues,pull_requests The token is fixed for the server process: after 1 hour calls fail with 401. Reconnect via /mcp. One repository per server. Work on another repository needs a session started there. Installation tokens cannot call user endpoints, so tools like get_me fail. The hosted GitHub MCP server and the claude.ai GitHub connector use your own identity, not the agent’s.
data.agent-token#agent-token:
agent-token org/repo prints a 1h agent token for that repository agent-token --login logs in via the login app's device flow (interactive) agent-token --check exits 1 unless a login is cached agent-token --permissions org/repo prints the permissions GitHub granted that token (JSON) agent-token --version prints the version (from v0.7.0) The login token is cached in ~/.cache/agent-token/login.json (mode 600) for 8 hours. A token per repository is reused until 5 minutes before it expires. Needs TOKEN_BROKER_URL. The login app’s client ID comes from the broker (GET /login-app); LOGIN_APP_CLIENT_ID overrides it.
Calls other than --login set AGENT_TOKEN_NONINTERACTIVE=1 and fail with run: agent-token --login instead of waiting for a device code nobody sees.
data.agent-token-git-credential#agent-token-g: A git credential helper that answers github.com requests with an agent token for the requested repository and stays silent for other hosts. It answers quit=1 when it has no token, so no later helper answers instead. It needs credential.useHttpPath=true, otherwise git sends no path. The system git config is in Use the scripts in your own image.

Variables the client scripts and agent-run read.
Variable Used by Meaning TOKEN_BROKER_URL agent-token and the scripts built on it Broker URL. Required. LOGIN_APP_CLIENT_ID agent-token Overrides the login app client ID that the broker serves at /login-app. AGENT_TOKEN_NONINTERACTIVE agent-token 1 fails instead of starting a device flow. Set by the other scripts. XDG_CACHE_HOME agent-token, agent-run Base of the cache directory; default ~/.cache. The cache is /agent-token. AGENT_COMMIT_MODE agent-commit local runs plain git commit; default api. GH_REPO agent-gh Target repository, as for gh. AGENT_APP_SLUG agent-run Slug of the agent app. Required. AGENT_IMAGE agent-run Image to run; default localhost/agent-sandbox:latest. AGENT_PODMAN_ARGS agent-run Extra podman run flags. CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY agent-run Passed into the container for Claude Code’s authentication.
data.where-the-broker-url-comes-from#Where th: Claude Code plugin: TOKEN_BROKER_URL, else the plugin option broker_url, else the Actions variable AGENT_TOKEN_BROKER_URL of the organization (never the repository), read with your gh. Dev Container: AGENT_TOKEN_BROKER_URL and AGENT_LOGIN_CLIENT_ID are read on the host and passed in as TOKEN_BROKER_URL and LOGIN_APP_CLIENT_ID; see Dev Container. Everything else: set TOKEN_BROKER_URL yourself.

data: Method and path Purpose Audience POST /token Agent token for a developer login token or an Actions OIDC token internal POST /token/actions Agent token for an Actions OIDC token only may be public GET /login-app Client ID of the login app internal GET /healthz Liveness probes GET /readyz Readiness probes GET /metrics Prometheus metrics scrapers
data.get-readyz#GET /readyz: 200 when GitHub accepts the app key (the broker calls GET /app with an app JWT, 3 second timeout), else 503 not ready.
data.post-token#POST /token:
Request:
POST /token Authorization: Bearer Content-Type: application/json {"repo": "my-org/my-repo"} The bearer token decides the path: a token with two dots is a GitHub Actions OIDC token, anything else is a user token of the login app. The body is limited to 4096 bytes.
Response (200):
{"token": "ghs_...", "expires_at": "2026-01-01T12:00:00Z", "permissions": {"contents": "write"}} The token covers the one repository and lives one hour. Errors are plain-text bodies:
Status Cause 400 Invalid JSON, or repo is not owner/name 401 Missing bearer token, invalid or unreadable Actions OIDC token, invalid login token 403 Repository outside GITHUB_ORG; app not installed on the repository; Actions token for a different repository or subject; ref or workflow not allowed; the developer has no push access 500 Signing the app JWT failed 502 GitHub failed: login token check, installation lookup, permission lookup or token minting For a login token the broker issues a token only if the developer has write or admin access to the repository. For an Actions token both the repository and the sub claim must name the requested repository, and any configured ref and workflow allowlists must match.
data.post-tokenactions#POST /token/actions: Same request and response as /token, but a bearer token that is not shaped like a JWT gets 401 only GitHub Actions OIDC tokens are accepted here. Forward only this path on a public route.

data:
The broker exports Prometheus metrics at GET /metrics. Instruments are named the OpenTelemetry way, and the Prometheus exporter turns each name into underscores and adds unit and type suffixes. In the chart, metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled renders a ServiceMonitor.
OpenTelemetry Prometheus Type Unit broker.token.requests broker_token_requests_total counter broker.token.duration broker_token_duration_seconds histogram (_bucket, _sum, _count) seconds Both carry two attributes:
Attribute Values outcome issued, unauthenticated, bad_request, denied, error via actions (Actions OIDC token), device (login token), unknown (rejected before the caller is known) broker.token.requests counts token requests by outcome. broker.token.duration records how long they took. Requests to /token/actions without a JWT-shaped bearer token count as unauthenticated via actions and record no duration.
The exporter also adds otel_scope_* labels and a target_info series, and the default Prometheus registry’s Go runtime and process metrics are served alongside.

Releases are tags vX.Y.Z on main. The releases page lists what changed in each and carries the assets: the signed container image is published to ghcr.io/pflege-de-labs/token-broker, and every release attaches the client scripts as agent-token-<version>.tar.gz with a checksums.txt.
The Helm chart is versioned separately and published to oci://ghcr.io/pflege-de-labs/charts when version in its Chart.yaml changes on main.
This documentation is versioned too: pick the version you run from the Versions menu.
